text.headline: The History of Evolvable Hardware
text.text: From the earliest visions of evolved electronics to the modern open-source revival — trace the key milestones in intrinsic analog evolvable hardware research.

text.headline: Early Vision
text.text:
Hugo de Garis describes embryological electronics and suggests that complex circuits could be "grown" through evolutionary search, laying the conceptual groundwork for evolvable hardware.

He postulated that evolutionary algorithms "will probably lead to electronic circuits being 'grown' in special hardware."

text.headline: Field Named
text.text:
De Garis and Tetsuya Higuchi formally coin evolvable hardware (EHW), defining it as the application of evolutionary algorithms to hardware during design or operation.

The tool of choice: the field programmable gate array (FPGA) — whose physically reprogrammable architecture can emulate candidate circuits evaluated by evolutionary algorithms.

text.headline: Sussex Breakthroughs
text.text:
Adrian Thompson at the University of Sussex evolves a series of circuits that canonize the evolutionary approach to analog circuit design.

His most famous result: a tone discriminator — a fully analog FPGA circuit that distinguishes between 1 kHz and 10 kHz tones using only 42 configurable logic blocks, exploiting latent device physics that would be abstracted away in simulation.

text.headline: XC6200 Retired
text.text:
Xilinx discontinues the openly documented XC6200 series FPGA — the only platform with a publicly available bitstream format. For cost and security reasons, FPGA manufacturers move to encrypted bitstreams.

Without complete knowledge of bitstream formats, intrinsic analog EHW research is effectively halted. The field enters a prolonged period of stagnation.

Read more →

media.caption: The Xilinx XC6216 — the FPGA that enabled early EHW

text.headline: Project IceStorm
text.text:
Reverse-engineering work unveiled the full Lattice iCE40 bitstream at the Chaos Communication Congress in Hamburg, Germany. The iCE40 — an ultra-low power, economy-grade FPGA — now has a fully documented bitstream format.

Although the reverse-engineering was not motivated by EHW research, it restores a modern, open substrate for intrinsic experiments after a 15-year gap.

Read more →

text.headline: Field Resurrected
text.text:
The ALIFE 2021 paper "Resurrecting FPGA Intrinsic Analog Evolvable Hardware" reproduces seminal analog behaviors on iCE40 devices and introduces an open-source experimentation stack.

The project is named BitstreamEvolution, built on the iCEstick HX1K development board using the Project IceStorm toolchain.

Read more →

text.headline: Robust Analog Evolution Demonstrated
text.text: The Artificial Life journal paper "Intrinsic Evolution of Analog Circuits Using Field Programmable Gate Arrays" details evolved amplitude maximization and pulse oscillation circuits plus robustness studies, formalizing the Bitstream Evolution roadmap.

text.headline: CoBEA Framework
text.text:
The GECCO '22 paper "CoBEA: framework for evolving hardware by direct manipulation of FPGA bitstreams" debuts an integrated stack that unifies low-level bitstream mutation, device communication, and on-board evaluation.

Enables >100× faster iCE40 reconfiguration and lowers the barrier to intrinsic experiments.

text.headline: Bitstream Evolution Toolkit Published
text.text:
The IEEE Access paper "Bitstream Evolution: an Open-Source FPGA Intrinsic Evolvable Hardware Toolkit" packages the hardware, software, and processes so new teams can evolve analog FPGA circuits.

Extends published experiments with deeper analyses on circuit robustness, transferability, and sensitivity to environmental shifts.

Read more →

text.headline: Port to pico2-ice & iCEFARM
text.text:
The Bitstream Evolution toolkit is ported to the pico2-ice development board, combining an RP2350 microcontroller with an iCE40 UP5K FPGA on a single board.

A new parallel evaluation system — iCEFARM — enables simultaneous evaluation across multiple boards, supporting larger population sizes and faster evolutionary runs.
